n: Samuel's prophetic word reaches all Israel. Meanwhile Israel fights the Philistines, a powerful coastal people. The armies camp at Eben-ezer and Aphek, near the edge of Israel's hill country.

f.g: A sea people who settled on the southern coast of Canaan, with five main cities and advanced iron weapons.
“Stone of help”; this place may be named in anticipation of a later victory.

n: The Philistines line up for battle and defeat Israel, killing about four thousand soldiers.
The elders ask the right question — why did the Lord let us lose? — but reach the wrong answer. Instead of repenting, they decide to bring the ark as a kind of good-luck charm.

f.g: The sacred gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law, symbol of God's presence.
They speak of the ark, not the Lord, as their savior.

n: They bring the ark from Shiloh. It represented the throne of the Lord, enthroned above the cherubim. Ominously, Eli's wicked sons come with it.

f.g: Cherubim are heavenly beings; two gold cherubim on the ark's lid framed the mercy seat, where God's presence was manifest.

n: When the ark arrives, Israel's army shouts so loudly the ground seems to shake. But excitement is not the same as faithfulness.
The Philistines hear the uproar and learn that the ark of Israel's God has come into the Hebrew camp.

f.g: A name often used by foreigners for the Israelites.

n: The Philistines panic, thinking a god has entered the camp. They had never faced anything like this before.
They remember the stories of the plagues on Egypt. Their pagan view shows in speaking of Israel's “Gods,” plural — they assume Israel worships many gods like they do.

f.w: the Gods that smote the Egyptians

n: Their leaders rally them: fight like men or become slaves to the Hebrews, as the Hebrews had been to them. Fear turns into fierce determination.
Israel suffers a far worse defeat — thirty thousand foot soldiers fall. Without righteousness, the sacred symbol could not save them.
The unthinkable happens: the ark is captured, and Hophni and Phinehas are killed on the same day, just as prophesied.
A Benjaminite runner races to Shiloh with his clothes torn and dust on his head — signs of mourning that announce bad news before he speaks.

f.w: with his clothes rent, and with earth upon his head
f.g: Traditional signs of grief and disaster.

n: Eli sits by the road anxiously waiting. Notice his greatest fear is for the ark of God. When the runner tells the news, the whole town cries out.
Hearing the uproar, Eli asks what is happening, and the messenger hurries to him.
The narrator reminds us that Eli is ninety-eight and blind, which explains why he must ask and why the news hits him so hard.
The messenger explains he has just fled from the battle. Eli asks gently, “What happened, my son?”
The news comes in four blows, each worse: Israel fled, many were killed, Eli's sons are dead, and — worst of all — the ark of God is taken.
At the mention of the ark, Eli falls backward, breaks his neck, and dies. He had judged Israel forty years. His tragic end shows that his heart did care for God's things, despite his failures.

f.g: This is the same Hebrew root as “glory” in verse 21 — a wordplay.
Eli served as both high priest and judge.

n: Phinehas's pregnant wife hears the news and goes into sudden, difficult labor.
As she is dying, the midwives try to comfort her with news of a son, normally great joy, but she does not respond. Her grief is too deep.
She names the boy Ichabod, meaning “no glory” or “where is the glory?”, because God's glory seemed to have left Israel along with the ark.

f.g: Hebrew “Where is the glory?” or “No glory.”

n: Her final words repeat the heart of the tragedy: the glory has departed because the ark is taken. Yet the following chapters show God's glory was never really defeated.

f.w: the ark of God is taken
